paras: The lynching of Ben Robertson took place in the town of Jeanerette, Louisiana, in late September or early October 1881, when a group of armed men took Robertson, a Black man jailed on a charge of chicken stealing, out of the town jail at night, flogged him and killed him. Early reports said he was hanged, but the paper that first said so later corrected itself to say he was shot while running away. Three men were charged with his murder and held on bond, and Louisiana editors condemned the killing as mob law.

Robertson, described as "a colored man," was arrested and confined in the town jail at Jeanerette on a charge of stealing chickens. The Chief's state-news column placed Jeanerette in Iberia parish, while its editorial and a later brief put it in St. Mary parish.

During the night a crowd broke into the jail and took Robertson out. According to the Donaldsonville Chief and the Sugar Bowl, the men whipped him, and when he broke away and ran he was shot dead. The New Iberia Star, citing a citizen of the town and the preliminary examination, wrote that "a number of men, all armed" threatened to hang him with a rope over his shoulders, and that when he freed himself and ran, "some one fired and killed him." The papers do not say where outside the jail he was flogged and shot.

The parish coroner, Dr. T. J. Woolf, held an inquest on the body and returned a verdict that the Star described as "in accordance with the facts stated," which at that point was the hanging version. On a Friday before October 22, Optime Schexnayder, Nicholas Provost Jr. and L. P. Provost were arrested at Jeanerette and charged with Robertson's murder. After a preliminary examination each was required to give a $500 bond to appear at the next term of the District Court. No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The story spread through Louisiana weeklies by way of the two Iberia papers, the Sugar Bowl and the New Iberia Star. The Sugar Bowl, quoted by the Baton Rouge Louisiana Capitolian on October 15, said the killing happened "under circumstances which deserve investigation" and that if a mob had broken open the jail, "they should be punished." The Star's first item, headed "Hung by a Mob" in the Richland Beacon, called the act "very felonious" and asked why a man should "perish for stealing a few chickens, when so many others are liberated for darker crimes."

The Donaldsonville Chief went furthest, running an editorial titled "Lynch Law" that called the killing a "dastardly crime" by "cowardly perpetrators" and warned readers who would "wink at the methods of Judge Lynch" that the precedent was dangerous. The Star's own correction, reprinted in the Lake Charles Commercial on October 22 under "Shot, Not Hung," struck a different note, describing Robertson as "of a malignant character" and "a first-class culprit" while conceding that "the matter was a little precipitated." The uncorrected hanging version kept circulating, appearing as a one-line note in the Brenham Weekly Banner in Texas on October 20 and in the St. Landry Democrat as late as November 12.

Accounts differ on how Robertson died: the Star's first report said he was hanged, while the Chief, the Sugar Bowl and the Star's later correction said he was shot while running from the men. The correction is the stronger evidence, since the Star retracted its own report on the word of a local citizen and the preliminary examination, and the Chief also judged the shooting version "more probable." The parish is also given two ways, but the Iberia Star's report that the coroner "of our parish" held the inquest supports Iberia.

bases: A group of men took a Black prisoner held for chicken stealing out of the Jeanerette jail at night, flogged him and killed him (A1, A3, A6).

Robertson was taken from jail by 'a number of men, all armed' and killed, whether shot while fleeing (A1, A3, A6) or hanged (A5); three men were charged with his murder (A6, A7), and the act punished an accused chicken thief outside the law (A2, A5).
The Sugar Bowl (via A3), the Iberia Star (A5, A6) and the Chief's state-news column (A1) agree that a mob took Robertson from the jail and killed him, though they differ on the manner of death.

accounts.gist: Ben was taken from the town jail by a mob, whipped, and shot and killed when he ran; the paper said the circumstances 'deserve investigation'.

accounts.label: Iberia Star, first report

accounts.gist: Armed men took him out and threatened to hang him with a rope over his shoulders; he freed himself and ran, and 'some one fired and killed him'.

accounts.label: Donaldsonville Chief
accounts.gist: Taken out and flogged, then shot dead when he broke away; the editorial noted the hanging report but judged the shooting version more probable.

framing.detail: The Chief's editorial 'Lynch Law' called it a 'dastardly crime' by 'cowardly perpetrators' and mob rule 'a crying evil and a disgrace to our country'.
The Iberia Star's first item, 'Hung by a Mob', called the act 'very felonious' and said 'This mob law should not be tolerated'.
The Star's correction called the victim 'of a malignant character' and 'a first-class culprit' while allowing the matter was 'a little precipitated'.
The Sugar Bowl said the killing deserved investigation and that a mob breaking open the jail 'should be punished'.
The Brenham Banner in Texas and the St. Landry Democrat carried the uncorrected hanging version as a brief.

versions.value: Flogged, broke away and was shot dead while running
Taken out by a mob and hanged

conflicts.note: The Iberia Star itself retracted its hanging report ('Shot, not hung') on the word of a Jeanerette citizen and the preliminary examination (A6); the Chief judged the shooting version 'more probable' (A2). The hanging version kept circulating in reprints (A4, A8).
The Iberia Star's statement that the coroner 'of our parish' held the inquest (A5) is the more local evidence for Iberia.
